400.title: Never alone
400.hook: when you shut the door and darken the room, you're not alone: God is within, and your own spirit (Discourses 1.14)
400.carry: a guardian spirit who never sleeps
400.howItsDone: Some readers of Epictetus use this chapter as a nighttime reminder, treating the private, unseen hours as just as real as the public ones.

segments.voice: Yesterday: adelphos, the servant as kin, and your line, look where your eyes are pointed. Were you gentle with someone who served you? Day four hundred. Four hundred days on the hill.

Late at night, door shut, lights off, phone face down. Nobody can see you. This is the hour when people eat the thing they swore off, send the message they'll regret, or lie awake feeling more alone than they've felt all day. It feels like the one hour that doesn't count, because no one is watching. Epictetus told his students that the dark room is never as empty as it looks. Today: never alone.
screen: `DOOR SHUT, LIGHTS OFF.` → `THE HOUR THAT DOESN'T COUNT.` → `THE ROOM ISN'T EMPTY.`

segments.voice: This is Discourses book one, chapter fourteen. A student asks: can a person really believe God sees everything they do? Epictetus answers with the whole world. Don't you see, he says, that everything is bound together? Plants bloom and bear fruit in their season, as if at a signal. Living things change with the moon and the sun. If plants and our bodies are that closely linked to the whole, how much more our minds, which for the Stoics are pieces of the same reason that runs it all. Then comes the image. God, he says, has set beside each person a guardian spirit, a daimon, who never sleeps and can't be fooled. So when you've shut your doors and made it dark inside, remember never to say you're alone. You're not. God is within, and your own spirit is within, and they need no light to see what you're doing. For the Stoics, this God isn't only someone peering in from outside. God is also the reason in you, which is never off duty. The chapter ends with a soldier's oath: soldiers swear loyalty to the emperor, Epictetus says, and we should swear an oath to God too, never to disobey and never to find fault with what we've been given. A neighbor tradition has its own words for the dark. A psalm in the King James words says, "If I say, Surely the darkness shall cover me; even the night shall be light about me." The two aren't the same teaching, and each is held on its own terms. In the psalm, darkness hides nothing from God. In Epictetus, the witness is already inside the room.
screen: `EVERYTHING IS BOUND TOGETHER.` · `A GUARDIAN WHO NEVER SLEEPS.` · `DOORS SHUT, YOU'RE NOT ALONE.` · `A SOLDIER'S OATH.` · then, large: `NEVER ALONE.`

segments.voice: If you can, find a quiet room and close the door. Dim the light if you like. Sit, and let the breath slow. Notice the feeling of being unseen. Then, in whatever way fits what you believe, notice that you're still here with yourself: the part of you that watches, that knows what you're doing, that never quite switches off. Sit with that company for a while. Nothing to hide from it, nothing to perform for it. The bell holds the time.
Never alone. Epictetus' reminder for the dark room: God is within, and your own guardian spirit, and neither needs light to see.
Your line: a guardian spirit who never sleeps. Tonight, when the door is shut and no one can see, act the way you would if the room were full. Day four hundred.

401.title: Blind, not wicked
401.hook: would you be angry with a blind man? then pity the one blind about good and bad (Discourses 1.18)
401.howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners reframe a person who has wronged them as mistaken about what is good, which can soften anger without excusing the harm.

segments.voice: Yesterday: never alone, the dark room that isn't empty, and your line, a guardian spirit who never sleeps. How did the unseen hours go? Day four hundred one.

Someone bumps your cart hard in the grocery store and keeps walking. You turn, ready to say something, and see the white cane. The bump is exactly as hard as it was a second ago. The only thing that's different is what you now understand about the person. Your shin still stings just the same. Epictetus asks: what if you understood everyone who wrongs you that way? Today: blind, not wicked.
screen: `A HARD BUMP IN THE AISLE.` → `THEN YOU SEE THE CANE.` → `WHAT IF YOU SAW EVERYONE THAT WAY?`

segments.voice: Discourses book one, chapter eighteen: that we ought not to be angry with the mistakes of others. Epictetus starts from something he thinks is true of all of us. Every person agrees with what seems true to them and reaches for what seems good to them. No one does wrong while thinking, this is bad for me, and I want it anyway. So when someone steals or cheats, what's actually happened? They've misjudged. They think the stolen thing is good for them, and they're wrong about what's good. That's the whole diagnosis. Now his students push back. But they're thieves! Robbers! Shouldn't such a person be put to death? And Epictetus says: then say it accurately. Shouldn't this person, who has been deceived about the most important things, who is blind, not in the eyes that tell white from black, but in the judgment that tells good from bad, be put to death? Say it that way, he says, and you'll hear how harsh it is. You wouldn't call for the blind or the deaf to be punished for not seeing or hearing. Pity them instead. Show them the mistake, and you may see them stop. This doesn't mean pretending harm didn't happen, or that no one should be held to account. Epictetus is talking about anger, the heat inside you. His claim is that the heat rests on a picture of the other person as wicked by choice, and that the picture is usually wrong.
screen: `EVERYONE REACHES FOR WHAT SEEMS GOOD.` · `THE WRONGDOER HAS MISJUDGED.` · `BLIND IN JUDGMENT, NOT IN EYES.` · `PITY, NOT ANGER.` · then, large: `BLIND, NOT WICKED.`

segments.voice: Sit and breathe. Bring to mind someone who has wronged you, not the worst person in your life, just someone who's annoyed you lately. Picture what they did. Now ask: what did they think was good, when they did it? Comfort, safety, being right, getting ahead? See them reaching for it, and missing. Notice if the heat in your chest shifts, even a little, toward something like pity. If it doesn't, that's all right. Just keep looking. The bell holds the time.
Blind. Epictetus' word for the wrongdoer: not wicked by choice, but blind in the judgment that tells good from bad, and owed pity more than anger.
Your line: pity them instead. The next time someone wrongs you today, try seeing them as someone who misjudged what was good, and try pity instead of anger once. Day four hundred one.

402.title: The clay lamp
402.hook: a thief took his iron lamp, so he bought a clay one, and the thief lost more (Discourses 1.18)
402.howItsDone: Many readers keep Epictetus' clay lamp as a shorthand for letting small losses go: replacing what's gone simply and refusing to give up their own calm or character over it.

segments.voice: Yesterday: blind, not wicked, the wrongdoer who misjudged what's good, and your line, pity them instead. Did you manage pity instead of anger, even once? Day four hundred two.

Someone takes the package off your porch. Someone swipes your bike, your lunch from the office fridge, your parking spot. It's small, but it stings for days. You replay it. You check the doorbell camera. You tell five people. Epictetus had something stolen too, and his reaction is one of the most famous little stories in the Discourses. It involves a noise at the window, an empty spot by the shrine, and a trip to buy a cheaper replacement. Today: lychnos.
screen: `THE PACKAGE OFF YOUR PORCH.` → `IT STINGS FOR DAYS.` → `A NOISE AT THE WINDOW.`

segments.voice: Still in Discourses book one, chapter eighteen, right after yesterday's teaching about blindness. Epictetus tells his students: I kept an iron lamp beside the little shrine of my household gods. I heard a noise at the window, ran down, and found the lamp gone. And then, he says, I thought it over. The thief wanted a lamp; that's understandable. So tomorrow, I told myself, you'll find a clay one. A person only loses what they have. Notice the arithmetic. An iron lamp was a decent possession. A clay lamp costs very little, and gives the same light. Epictetus lost almost nothing that mattered. The thief, as Epictetus sees it elsewhere in the Discourses, paid a much higher price: for a lamp, he became a thief. He gave up his own honesty, his trustworthiness, which no one could have taken from him, in exchange for a piece of iron. Who lost more? Epictetus also explains why we get so angry at thieves: because we admire the things they take. If you didn't prize your clothes so much, he says, you wouldn't rage at the one who steals them. And there's a funny ending to the story, from outside the Discourses. The writer Lucian, a generation later, mocks a man who paid three thousand drachmas for Epictetus' clay lamp after the philosopher died, as if owning it would make him wise. The cheap lamp became an expensive treasure, which is exactly the kind of admiring Epictetus warned about.
screen: `THE IRON LAMP, STOLEN.` · `TOMORROW, A CLAY ONE.` · `FOR A LAMP, HE BECAME A THIEF.` · `THE CLAY LAMP SOLD FOR A FORTUNE.` · then, large: `A CLAY LAMP.`

segments.voice: Sit and breathe. Think of one small thing that was taken from you, recently or long ago: an object, some money, credit for your work, a seat. Notice how tightly you're still holding it. Now picture the clay lamp: a simple, cheap thing that gives the same light. What would your clay lamp be here? Let yourself buy it, in your mind. Then notice what you still have that no one could take. The bell holds the time.
Lychnos. Greek for the lamp Epictetus lost: an iron one, replaced for a little with a cheap clay lychnos, while the thief gave up his own honesty.
Your line: a clay lamp. If something small is taken from you today, let it go and buy the clay lamp: replace it simply, and keep what can't be stolen. Day four hundred two.

403.title: Not my judgment
403.hook: the tyrant has power over the body, never the judgment (Discourses 1.19)
403.howItsDone: Some Stoic readers sort a fear into what it could touch and what it can't, keeping their attention on their own judgment and choices.

segments.voice: Yesterday: lychnos, and your line, a clay lamp. Was there something small you let go of? Day four hundred three.

Epictetus' old master, Epaphroditus, once sold a slave who made shoes, because he thought the man was useless. Then the shoemaker was bought by someone in the emperor's household and became the emperor's own shoemaker. Suddenly Epaphroditus couldn't do enough for him. How is our dear Felicio, he'd ask. And if you came looking for Epaphroditus, you'd be told he was in a meeting with Felicio. Epictetus tells it with a straight face, and lets it sit. Today: dogma.
screen: `THE USELESS SHOEMAKER.` → `NOW HE WORKS FOR THE EMPEROR.` → `IN A MEETING WITH FELICIO.`

segments.voice: This is Discourses book one, chapter nineteen: how we should behave toward tyrants. Felicio is the joke that opens the door. Why did Epaphroditus suddenly fawn over his old shoemaker? Not because Felicio changed. Because Felicio was now near the emperor. Then Epictetus asks the real question. What is it that frightens people? The tyrant and his guards? No. Nothing that is free by nature can be troubled by anything but itself. What troubles us is our own judgments. So when the tyrant says, I'll chain your leg, the person who prizes the leg begs for mercy. The person who prizes their own will says: if it seems better to you, chain it. Take the body, if you have power over it. But no one, Epictetus says, has power over another person's will. They can threaten. They can make choosing costly. But the choosing stays with you. Tyrants come in small sizes, too: a boss who controls your schedule, a relative who controls the family's approval, an online crowd that controls how you feel about yourself. Epictetus' question works on all of them. What exactly can they touch? Your paycheck, maybe. Your mood, only if you hand it over. Your judgment: never. That's not a promise that standing firm will be painless. It's a map of where the fight actually is.
screen: `WHY FAWN OVER FELICIO?` · `OUR OWN JUDGMENTS FRIGHTEN US.` · `THE TYRANT CAN'T REACH THE WILL.` · `TYRANTS IN SMALL SIZES.` · then, large: `NOT MY JUDGMENT.`

segments.voice: Sit and breathe. Name one fear that's been pressing on you lately: losing a job, someone's disapproval, a diagnosis, money. Say it plainly to yourself. Now sort it. What could this actually touch? Write the list in your mind: my income, my plans, my comfort, my body. Then name what it can't touch: what I value, how I treat people, whether I stay honest. Rest your attention on that second list for the rest of the sit. The bell holds the time.
Dogma. Greek for judgment, a settled opinion: Epictetus' word for the views that shape our reactions, which no tyrant can touch.
Your line: the choosing stays with you. When someone with power over you leans on you today, ask quietly what they can touch, and remind yourself: the choosing stays with you. Day four hundred three.

404.title: Test the coin
404.hook: test each impression the way a money-changer tests coins (Discourses 1.20)
404.carry: an impression is a coin someone has passed you
404.howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners pause on a strong first impression, asking whether it's a fact or an interpretation, before acting on it, a habit some trace to this chapter.

segments.voice: Yesterday: dogma, Felicio the shoemaker and the tyrant who can't reach the mind, and your line, the choosing stays with you. Which fear did you sort? Day four hundred four.

Hand a cashier a hundred-dollar bill and watch. They hold it up to the light. They run a pen across it. They feel the paper between finger and thumb. Nobody's offended; it's just what you do with money, because fakes exist. Now think how many thoughts you accepted today without holding a single one up to the light. Epictetus noticed the same mismatch in the markets of his own time. Today: money-changer.
screen: `HELD UP TO THE LIGHT.` → `BECAUSE FAKES EXIST.` → `HOW MANY THOUGHTS DID YOU CHECK?`

segments.voice: This is Discourses book one, chapter twenty, on reason examining itself. Every skill, Epictetus says, looks at something outside itself. The cobbler looks at leather, the musician at sound. Reason is the one faculty that can look at itself, and at the impressions that come to it. And then he goes to the market. Look at the money-changer, the person whose job is to test coins. For coins, he says, we've invented a whole craft. The tester uses sight. He uses touch. He even uses smell. And last of all, hearing: he drops the coin on the counter and listens to it ring. Not once. Again and again, until his ear is as trained as a musician's. Where people think a mistake would cost them, Epictetus says, they bring every sense to bear. But with the impressions that come to the mind, the passing thought that someone is insulting you, that you're a failure, that you need this thing right now, we yawn and accept whatever is handed to us. Epictetus calls this the philosopher's first and greatest work: to test impressions, and let none in untested. An impression is a coin someone has passed you. It might be real. It might be lead painted gold. Before you spend it, before you act on it, say it, or let it set your mood, you can turn it over, hold it to the light, and drop it on the counter to hear how it rings.
screen: `REASON LOOKS AT ITSELF.` · `THE MONEY-CHANGER'S SENSES.` · `THOUGHTS ACCEPTED WITH A YAWN.` · `HEAR HOW IT RINGS.` · then, large: `TEST THE COIN.`

segments.voice: Sit and breathe. Let the next thought that shows up be the coin on the counter: a worry, a judgment about someone, a plan. Don't spend it yet. Look at it: is it a fact, or a story about a fact? Feel its weight: is it heavier than it needs to be? Listen to it ring: does it sound true, or a little hollow? Then set it down, and wait for the next one. The bell holds the time.
Money-changer. Epictetus' image for testing the mind: the market worker who checks a coin by sight, touch, smell and the ring of its drop, before letting it pass.
Your line: an impression is a coin someone has passed you. Before you act on one strong thought today, hold it up to the light and listen to how it rings. Day four hundred four.

405.title: A good opponent
405.hook: difficulties show who we are, like a trainer pairing you with a rough young wrestler (Discourses 1.24)
405.carry: what is this making of me
405.howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners reframe a difficulty as a training partner, asking what virtue it calls on, a habit drawn from this chapter's wrestling image.

segments.voice: Yesterday: money-changer, listening for the ring, and your line, an impression is a coin someone has passed you. Which thought did you hold up to the light before spending it? Day four hundred five.

In a boxing gym, the coach looks over the new kid and pairs him, on purpose, not with the easiest partner but with someone a little rougher, a little stronger, someone who makes him sweat and sometimes puts him down. He goes home sore and annoyed. A few months on, he moves differently. Epictetus took that gym wisdom and pointed it at the hardest things in life. Today: sparring partner.
screen: `THE COACH PAIRS HIM ROUGHER.` → `SORE AND ANNOYED.` → `A FEW MONTHS ON.`

segments.voice: This is Discourses book one, chapter twenty-four, on how to struggle with circumstances. It opens with a short line: it's difficulties that show what people are. Not comfortable days. Hard ones. And then the picture. When a difficulty lands on you, Epictetus says, remember that God, like a wrestling trainer, has paired you with a rough young opponent. Why? So that you can become an Olympic champion. And that doesn't happen without sweat. Then he says something bold. No one, he tells his student, has ever been handed a better difficulty than yours, if you're willing to use it the way an athlete uses a tough sparring partner. Notice what he's not saying. He isn't saying the difficulty is good in itself, or that you deserved it, or that suffering is secretly pleasant. The opponent is rough. It hurts. What he's changing is the question. Instead of, why is this happening to me, he asks: what is this making of me? A sparring partner isn't your enemy, even when he puts you on the mat. He's how you find out what you've got, and how you get more of it. For the Stoics, the trainer is God, the reason that runs the world. Some readers keep that, and some keep only the gym. Either way, the hard conversation, the setback at work, the stubborn habit, all of them can be read as the partner your training needed.
screen: `DIFFICULTIES SHOW WHAT PEOPLE ARE.` · `THE TRAINER PAIRS YOU ROUGH.` · `NO BETTER DIFFICULTY THAN YOURS.` · `WHAT IS THIS MAKING OF ME?` · then, large: `A GOOD OPPONENT.`

segments.voice: Sit and breathe. Bring to mind one difficulty you're facing right now. Picture it, not as a wall, but as a rough young opponent across the mat. What is it testing? Patience, courage, honesty, endurance? Name the one muscle it's working. Then breathe, and let yourself step onto the mat, not happy about it, just willing. You don't have to win today. You just have to train. The bell holds the time.
Sparring partner. Epictetus' name for hardship: the rough partner a trainer chooses for you, so you find out what you've got, and grow it.
Your line: what is this making of me. When something hard meets you today, ask what it's training, and meet one difficulty as a sparring partner. Day four hundred five.

406.title: Stand firm
406.hook: the good lies in the will, so stand firm there (Discourses 1.29)
406.carry: let the branches move in the wind
406.howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners prepare for pressure by naming in advance what could be lost and what couldn't, and anchoring themselves in their own choices.

segments.voice: Yesterday: sparring partner, the rough partner the trainer chose, and your line, what is this making of me. What difficulty did you meet as training? Day four hundred six, the end of the week.

A tree in a storm doesn't stay still. The branches thrash, leaves tear off, the whole crown bends sideways. What keeps it standing is underneath, where you can't see: the roots, gripping the ground. A tree that tried to hold every leaf in place would snap. Epictetus has a whole chapter on constancy, on staying steady when pressure comes, and his advice runs the same way as the tree's. Know where your roots are. Today: stand firm.
screen: `A TREE IN A STORM.` → `BRANCHES THRASH, ROOTS HOLD.` → `KNOW WHERE YOUR ROOTS ARE.`

segments.voice: This is Discourses book one, chapter twenty-nine, on constancy. It opens with a short, dense claim. The good, Epictetus says, is a certain state of the will. So is the bad. And everything outside the will, money, health, reputation, even the body, is material the will works with. Earlier in the Discourses he puts it this way: as wood is the carpenter's material, each person's own life is the material of the art of living. The carpenter isn't good because the wood is fine; he's good because of what he does with it. That's where the roots are. If your good lives in your will, then pressure on everything else is weather in the branches. A threat to your job, your comfort, your standing: those are leaves. Real things, worth caring about, but not the roots. Epictetus then imagines the test. Someone powerful threatens you. Don't panic, he says; ask what is being threatened. If it's the body or the property, the will is still standing. He even pictures God calling a student forward as a witness: come and testify for me. Is anything outside the will good or bad? Will you show up and say it, or will you tremble and say the opposite? Constancy isn't stiffness. It isn't refusing to feel the wind. It's knowing which part of you is supposed to move and which part isn't. Look back at the week: never alone, blind, not wicked, a clay lamp, not my judgment, test the coin, a good opponent. And today, stand firm.
screen: `THE GOOD IS A STATE OF THE WILL.` · `EVERYTHING ELSE IS MATERIAL.` · `CALLED FORWARD AS A WITNESS.` · `NOT STIFFNESS: KNOWING THE ROOTS.` · then, large: `STAND FIRM.`

segments.voice: Sit with your feet flat on the floor. Feel the ground under you, solid. Breathe. Now bring to mind one pressure you're under: a deadline, a hard conversation, someone's expectations. Let it blow through you like wind. Notice what bends: plans, comfort, mood. Then come back to your feet on the floor, and to what doesn't need to bend: what you value, how you intend to act. Stay there, rooted. The bell holds the time.
Stand firm. Epictetus' constancy: the good lives in the will, so let the branches move in the wind and keep the roots where they are.
Your line: let the branches move in the wind. When pressure comes today, let what can bend, bend, and stay steady in the one place that's yours. Day four hundred six, and a week done.
